Text Message Scams

DVLA Vehicle Tax Text: Is It Genuine or a Scam?

A DVLA text asking you to confirm bank or payment details, or claim a vehicle-tax refund through a link, is a scam. Use GOV.UK directly instead.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-04-24 · Updated 2026-08-01 · 6 min read

Quick answer: A message asking for bank or card details, confirmation of payment details, or a vehicle-tax refund through a link is a scam — DVLA issues refunds automatically and will not ask you to confirm payment details. Genuine reminders do exist, so check and tax your vehicle only through GOV.UK, and forward scam texts to 7726.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What the fake DVLA tax text says

Fake DVLA texts commonly claim a vehicle-tax payment failed, tax is overdue, a penalty is imminent, or a refund is waiting. They direct the recipient to a GOV.UK-style copycat page that collects card, bank or identity details. In its April 2025 scam-awareness news story, DVLA said almost 20,000 customers called its contact centre in 2024 to report fraudulent activity.

DVLA's current advice makes the answer narrower and more reliable than judging the sender name: a message asking for bank or card details, confirmation of payment details, or a vehicle-tax refund through a link is the scam sign. DVLA will not ask for your bank-account details or ask you to confirm payment details, and vehicle-tax refunds are issued automatically — never via an email with a link. Genuine reminders do exist, so check and tax the vehicle only through GOV.UK.

Why a "DVLA" text is easy to fake

Scammers can use official-looking sender names, GOV.UK-style design, and urgent wording. Sender IDs can be spoofed, so DVLA showing as the sender proves nothing — the fake can even land in the same thread as a genuine message. Timing can also make a fake feel real if it arrives near a renewal date.

The key facts are clearer than the message: DVLA has said the only place to access official information on DVLA and its services is GOV.UK, that it never sends text messages about vehicle-tax refunds, and — per a DVLA official — that it never asks for bank or credit-card details by text message or email.

The same criminals run a phone version — an automated call claiming your tax payment failed — covered at DVLA Scam Calls: How to Spot a Fake Caller (UK).

What genuine DVLA reminders actually look like

Knowing the real process makes the fake obvious.

  • The standard tax-due reminder is a letter — the V11 — posted to the address on your V5C log book. GOV.UK also refers to reminders arriving by email or text, so a reminder in your inbox is not automatically fake — but a genuine one never asks for bank details.
  • If a Direct Debit payment fails through lack of funds, DVLA says the account holder gets an email and it retries within 4 working days; if that fails too, a further email says the Direct Debit is cancelled and the vehicle is no longer taxed. Note what is missing: no request for bank details, no urgent payment link.
  • A genuine refund is a cheque, issued automatically for any full months left once you tell DVLA the vehicle is sold, scrapped, exported or SORNed, sent to the address on the log book — nothing to claim, no link, no bank details.

Signs a "DVLA" text is a scam

  • It asks you to pay, update payment details, or claim a refund through a link.
  • The link is not on gov.uk, or it uses a lookalike, extra words, or a shortened URL.
  • It threatens a fine, penalty, or deadline if you do not act immediately.
  • It asks for card numbers, bank details, or personal information.
  • It claims a refund is waiting — genuine refunds arrive as automatic cheques, not links.
  • It asks you to upload or confirm driving-licence or V5C details. DVLA warns against sharing these online (identity-theft risk).
  • It looks official but asks you to use a route outside GOV.UK.

How the vehicle-tax scam works

First, a text claims a vehicle-tax payment failed, tax is due, or a refund is available. Second, it pushes you to a link. Third, the link opens a fake page styled to look like GOV.UK or DVLA. Fourth, it asks for card, bank, or personal details. Fifth, the criminals use those details to take money, attempt further card transactions, or target you again.

Some pages ask for a small "fee" to seem believable while harvesting details for larger fraud later.

How to check with DVLA safely

Close the message and type gov.uk yourself. Use:

  • gov.uk/check-vehicle-tax to check free whether a vehicle is taxed or SORNed — you only need the registration number. Records can take up to 2 working days to update after you tax.
  • gov.uk/vehicle-tax to tax a vehicle officially, using the reference from your V11 reminder, your V5C log book, or the green new-keeper slip.
  • gov.uk/vehicle-tax-refund to understand when a refund is issued automatically.

DVLA says it may ask a person to confirm personal details by email or text when there is a live enquiry, so 'DVLA never texts' is not a safe universal rule. The red line is a message asking for bank details, confirmation of payment details, or a vehicle-tax refund claim. If a message refers to a real enquiry, confirm it through a GOV.UK service or contact route you open yourself.

If you paid or shared card details

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the number on the back of your card. Tell them it was a scam, ask them to stop the card if needed, and ask about disputing the transaction. A card payment may be recoverable through chargeback, depending on the circumstances and card scheme rules.

Then take stock of what the fake page collected. Card details: watch statements for small "test" transactions. Name, address, date of birth or licence details: consider Cifas Protective Registration and monitor your credit reports with the agencies MoneyHelper lists — Experian, Equifax and TransUnion, the three main agencies, plus Crediva. Our scam recovery checklist walks through this in order.

How to report a DVLA text scam (UK)

Forward the text to 7726. Ofcom says forwarding scam texts to 7726 is free and alerts your mobile provider to investigate and block the number.

If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

If a similar scam arrived by email, forward it to report@phishing.gov.uk; DVLA also suggests reporting misleading copycat adverts to the search engine.

Frequently asked questions

Does DVLA send texts about vehicle tax refunds?

DVLA has said it never sends text messages about vehicle-tax refunds — a genuine refund is an automatic cheque to the address on your V5C. Treat any "refund waiting" link as a scam.

Does DVLA ask for bank or card details by text or email?

DVLA says it will never ask you for your bank-account details or ask you to confirm payment details. Use GOV.UK instead.

Does DVLA ever send genuine emails or texts at all?

Yes — which is why the sender name proves nothing. GOV.UK refers to tax reminders arriving by letter (the V11), email or text, and DVLA emails you if a Direct Debit fails. None of those ask for bank or payment details.

The text arrived when my tax was due - could it be genuine?

Timing proves nothing — scam texts go out in bulk. Ignore the link and check directly on GOV.UK.

A message says my Direct Debit for vehicle tax failed - what should I do?

Do not use anything in the message. Check the vehicle yourself at gov.uk/check-vehicle-tax, and retax at gov.uk/vehicle-tax if the tax really has lapsed.

I entered card details on a DVLA-style site - what now?

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the number on your card. Ask them to secure the card and dispute the payment. If you also gave personal details, consider Cifas Protective Registration. Then report the scam.

How do I report a fake DVLA text?

Forward it to 7726 (free). If you lost money or shared sensitive details, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.
